newsitem.title: UK: Bomb hoax mars trip by Prince Charles to N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Bomb hoax mars trip by Prince Charles to N.Ireland.

text.p: Explosives experts blew up a suspicious van near a concert hall in Belfast where Britain's Prince Charles was attending a gala on Tuesday but no bomb was found in the vehicle, police said.
"It was declared a hoax," a police spokeswoman told Reuters.

She said the van, which belonged to a flower company, had been hijacked and the driver had been told to drive to the city centre. Police in the area stopped the vehicle during a security check and the driver jumped out, shouting a bomb warning.
Police sealed off the area close to Belfast's showpiece 32 million pound ($52 million) Waterfront Hall by the banks of the River Lagan which the prince opened a few hours earlier.
The prince's bodyguards were alerted but the gala concert featuring opera singer Kiri Te Kanawa was not disrupted.
Security for the visit, the prince's first since Irish guerrillas stepped up a war on troops and police in the British-ruled province late last year, was increased.
He was accompanied by a large group of plain clothes bodyguards and uniformed police officers during open air functions earlier in the day.

The outlawed Irish Republican Army, fighting to end British rule, abandoned a 17-month truce in February 1996 with a series of bombs in London. In October the IRA launched a wave of attacks in Northern Ireland and has killed two soldiers since.
Charles has been a target for protests on previous trips to both sides of the divided island because he holds the largely ceremonial title of "colonel-in-chief" of the elite Parachute Regiment.
Paratroops shot dead 13 unarmed Irish nationalists during a Roman Catholic protest march in Londonderry city in 1972 in what became known as "Bloody Sunday".
Northern Ireland's Catholic minority say Britain should reopen an investigation into the killings and formally declare the victims innocent.
